claim: Primates make about four to five quick eye movements (saccades) every second.
source: Primates make about four to five quick eye movements (saccades) every second.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about primate eye movement behavior.

claim: The oculomotor system selects a new target to look at depending on the match between the content of the current visual scene and the subject's internal state and current goals.
source: Before each movement, the oculomotor system selects a new target to look at depending on the match between the content of the current visual scene and the subject's internal state and current goals, i.e., what, if anything, the subject is looking for (Itti and Koch, 2001; Theeuwes, 2010; Wolfe and Horowitz, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on visual attention and target selection.

claim: Saccades are strongly coupled to visuospatial attention.
source: Saccades are strongly coupled to visuospatial attention, which comprises a collection of mechanisms that regulate perception and thereby mediate the target selection process (Carrasco, 2011; Maunsell, 2015; Moore and Zirnsak, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the relationship between saccades and attention.

claim: Neurons implicated in attention control and saccade generation are typically found within the same circuits.
source: Neurons implicated in attention control and saccade generation are typically found within the same circuits.
evidence: This is a statement of established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The functional coupling between saccades and attention is bidirectional.
source: And importantly, the functional coupling between saccades and attention is bidirectional.
evidence: This claim is supported by the subsequent discussion of presaccadic attention and endogenous attention effects.

claim: Planning a saccade automatically commits attentional resources to the saccade endpoint such that perceptual processing is enhanced at that location.
source: On one hand, the planning of a saccade automatically commits attentional resources to the saccade endpoint such that perceptual processing is enhanced at that location. This phenomenon, known as presaccadic attention, is firmly supported by both psychophysical (Hoffman and Subramaniam, 1995; Kowler et al., 1995; Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Zhao et al., 2012) and neurophysiological experiments (Moore and Fallah, 2001; Moore and Fallah, 2004; Cavanaugh and Wurtz, 2004; Armstrong and Moore, 2007; Steinmetz and Moore, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to psychophysical and neurophysiological studies.

claim: Endogenous attention deployment increases the probability that a saccade will be directed to the attended point.
source: This is referred to as endogenous attention, and there is evidence that its deployment impacts subsequent eye movements in two ways: it increases the probability that a saccade will be directed to the attended point (Kustov and Robinson, 1996; Belopolsky and Theeuwes, 2009; Belopolsky and Theeuwes, 2012), and if fixation is maintained, it alters the temporal and spatial characteristics of microsaccades (Hafed and Clark, 2002; Engbert and Kliegl, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The attentional locus and saccade endpoint can be dissociated.
source: However, this link between endogenous attention and eye movements is not obligatory; the attentional locus and saccade endpoint can be dissociated (Katnani and Gandhi, 2013; Steinmetz and Moore, 2014; Klapetek et al., 2016), and microsaccades are only weak, unreliable markers of attentional allocation (Yu et al., 2022; Willett and Mayo, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The effects of directing covert attention or a saccade to a given location can be quite distinct in terms of the activated neuronal populations.
source: Furthermore, the effects of directing covert attention or a saccade to a given location can be quite distinct in terms of the activated neuronal populations (Ignashchenkova et al., 2004; Thompson et al., 2005; Armstrong et al., 2009), and may have slightly different perceptual consequences (for instance, on orientation or spatial frequency sensitivity; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Exogenous and endogenous signals acted at different times and independently of each other in urgent prosaccade and antisaccade tasks.
source: By analyzing performance in an urgent prosaccade task (look toward a cue) and an urgent antisaccade task (look away from a cue), we found that exogenous and endogenous signals acted at different times and independently of each other.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from earlier studies by the authors.

claim: Exogenous response to cue onset manifested as 'captured' saccades that occurred early (~100 ms after cue onset), were strongly stereotyped across individuals, highly sensitive to luminance, and largely impervious to task rules or top-down control.
source: Specifically, the exogenous response to the cue onset manifested as 'captured' saccades, eye movements toward the cue that were, by all accounts, involuntary: they occurred early (∼100 ms after cue onset), were strongly stereotyped across individuals, highly sensitive to luminance, and largely impervious to task rules or top-down control.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from earlier studies by the authors.

claim: The endogenous response manifested as a sustained rise toward high-performance accuracy that occurred slightly later (~150 ms after cue onset), was more variable across individuals, and was aligned with the task-defined goal.
source: In contrast, the endogenous response manifested as a sustained rise toward high-performance accuracy that was consistent with a deliberate process: the rise occured slightly later (∼150 ms after cue onset), it was more variable across individuals, and was aligned with the task-defined goal.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from earlier studies by the authors.

claim: Exogenous capture was minimized when the luminances of the cue and the non-cue were the same.
source: As intended, exogenous capture was minimized when the luminances of the cue and the non-cue were the same (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: For both pro and anti trials, the fraction correct hovers near 0.5 for processing times around 100 ms when cue and non-cue luminances are equal.
source: In this case, for both pro (panel a) and anti trials (panel b), the fraction correct hovers near 0.5 for processing times around 100 ms, which is when the exogenous effect would be expected to be strongest (Salinas et al., 2019; Goldstein et al., 2022; Oor et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and b, and by citations to prior work.

claim: Exogenous capture was reinstated when the cue and the non-cue differed in luminance.
source: Also as intended, exogenous capture was reinstated when the cue and the non-cue differed in luminance (Figure 2c and d), with the exogenous signal always biasing the saccades toward the high-luminance stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: In pro trials, the salient cue produced a sharp, transient increase in the probability of making a correct prosaccade, whereas the salient non-cue produced a sharp, transient decrease.
source: In pro trials (Figure 2c), the salient cue (dark curve) produced a sharp, transient increase in the probability of making a correct prosaccade, whereas the salient non-cue (light curve) produced a sharp, transient decrease.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: All capture effects were short-lived, peaking at rPT≈100 ms and mostly disappearing for rPT≳150 ms.
source: All of these capture effects were short-lived, peaking at rPT≈100 ms and mostly disappearing for rPT≳150 ms; thereafter, the endogenously driven rise toward asymptotic performance was, once again, basically the same across luminance conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the tachometric curves shown in Figure 2.

claim: Exogenous and endogenous influences are dissociable across processing time, and their effects on visuomotor performance are largely independent of each other.
source: These results confirm that exogenous and endogenous influences are dissociable across processing time, and that their effects on visuomotor performance are largely independent of each other.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results presented in Figure 2.

claim: The degree of exogenous capture varied quite dramatically across participants, from 0% to 100%.
source: With the resulting data arranged according to the magnitude of the effect, it is clear that the degree of exogenous capture varied quite dramatically across participants, from 0% to 100%.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of individual participant data shown in Figure 3b and d.

claim: The early exogenous signal always tracks the higher luminance stimulus, and the evoked exogenous response is the same regardless of the task rule.
source: This result confirms that the early exogenous signal always tracks the higher luminance stimulus, and that the evoked exogenous response is the same regardless of the task rule.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results showing symmetry of capture effects between pro and anti trials.

claim: Antisaccades consistently required more processing time than prosaccades to reach a comparable performance criterion.
source: Based on the data from these 11 participants, a comparison between rise points indicated that antisaccades consistently required more processing time than prosaccades to reach a comparable performance criterion (Figure 4c, circles).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The rPT cost of an endogenously guided antisaccade relative to an endogenously guided prosaccade is about 25–35 ms.
source: These results indicate that the rPT cost of an endogenously guided antisaccade relative to an endogenously guided prosaccade is about 25–35 ms, and support the hypothesis that saccade plans are, to a degree, obligatorily coupled to endogenous attention.
evidence: This claim is based on multiple analyses of the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: 15 of the 18 participants guessed predominantly toward the cue rather than toward the non-cue.
source: The results show that 15 of the 18 participants guessed predominantly toward the cue rather than toward the non-cue (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The expected processing-time cost is 27 ms for zero bias.
source: As indicated by the offset of the regression line in Figure 6c (dotted line), the expected cost is 27 ms for zero bias.
evidence: This claim is based on regression analysis of the data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The fraction of correct choices during the transition range was consistently higher for pro than for anti trials.
source: The answer is yes. The fraction of correct choices during the transition range was consistently higher for pro than for anti trials (Figure 7e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Generating a correct antisaccade requires about 30 ms more processing time than generating a correct prosaccade based on the same perceptual signal.
source: According to the measured time courses, generating a correct antisaccade requires about 30 ms more processing time than generating a correct prosaccade based on the same perceptual signal.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Saccade plans elaborated during fixation are biased toward the location where attention is endogenously deployed, but the coupling is weak and can be willfully overridden very rapidly.
source: The results indicate that saccade plans elaborated during fixation are biased toward the location where attention is endogenously deployed, but the coupling is weak and can be willfully overridden very rapidly.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The observed coupling between endogenous attention and saccade planning is consistent with prior studies showing that endogenous attention and saccade planning can be dissociated.
source: Consistent with data showing that endogenous attention and saccade planning can be dissociated (Ignashchenkova et al., 2004; Thompson et al., 2005; Armstrong et al., 2009; Steinmetz and Moore, 2014; Klapetek et al., 2016; Li et al., 2021), our results are indicative of coupling that is comparatively weak in this direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and comparison with the current results.

claim: The time costs for making an eye movement to an attended cue location versus to an unattended non-cue location observed by Belopolsky and Theeuwes, 2009 were remarkably similar to those in the current study, on the order of 20–40 ms.
source: In this regard, our results are comparable to those of Belopolsky and Theeuwes, 2009, who used a task in which participants made saccades to a target location that did or did not coincide with the location of an attended symbolic cue. They measured saccadic RTs that were much longer than in our case (roughly 500–800 ms), and yet their derived time costs for making an eye movement to an attended cue location versus to an unattended non-cue location were remarkably similar to ours, on the order of 20–40 ms.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with results from a cited study.

claim: When saccades are strongly biased (Experiments 3 and 4), the tachometric curves demonstrate the corresponding capture but then (briefly) go in the opposite direction.
source: Instead, when saccades are strongly biased (Experiments 3 and 4), the tachometric curves demonstrate the corresponding capture but then (briefly) go in the opposite direction. This can be seen in the pro curves of Experiment 3 (Figure 3a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 3c, dark blue traces) and in the anti curves of Experiment 4 (Figure 3c, Figure 2—figure supplement 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 3d, bright red traces); in both cases there is a sharp increase in accuracy during the capture window (approximately 83–124 ms) that is then partially offset immediately afterward, before the final rise toward asymptotic performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The exogenous response is automatically followed by a motor reaction in the opposite direction.
source: It is as if the exogenous response was automatically followed by a motor reaction in the opposite direction. Perhaps the oculomotor circuitry is such that an exogenous signal can rapidly trigger a saccade, but if it does not, then the corresponding motor plan is rapidly suppressed regardless of anything else.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed downward rebound in the tachometric curves.

claim: In both exogenous and endogenous cases, a shift of spatial attention activates a motor plan that is either executed within a few tens of milliseconds (to trigger a saccade) or is rapidly suppressed.
source: This idea suggests a symmetry with the effect of endogenous attention discussed in the previous paragraph: it appears that in both cases, exogenous and endogenous, a shift of spatial attention activates a motor plan that is either executed within a few tens of milliseconds (to trigger a saccade) or is rapidly suppressed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns in the data.

claim: Saccade trajectories could deviate either toward a distracter or away from it depending on the time at which the distracter was shown.
source: However, later studies showed that attention effects on saccade trajectories could be either repulsive or attractive (Van der Stigchel et al., 2006), and specifically demonstrated that saccade trajectories could deviate either toward a distracter or away from it depending on the time at which the distracter was shown (Theeuwes and Godijn, 2004; McSorley et al., 2006; Giuricich et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The fundamental factors that determine behavior in prosaccade/antisaccade tasks are the magnitudes of the resulting exogenous and endogenous signals, and whether they are aligned or misaligned.
source: We think that, more than the specific task instructions or the structure of the event sequence, the fundamental factors that determine behavior in all of these cases are the magnitudes of the resulting exogenous and endogenous signals, and whether they are aligned or misaligned.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' interpretation of their results and prior work.

claim: The spatial signal encoded by neurons in monkey prefrontal cortex during the antisaccade task can be accurately predicted from their stimulus- and saccade-related responses during a memory guided saccade task.
source: Furthermore, a recent study (Zhu et al., 2024) showed that the spatial signal encoded by neurons in monkey prefrontal cortex during the antisaccade task can be accurately predicted from their stimulus- and saccade-related responses during a simpler task that involves no spatial conflict whatsoever (a memory guided saccade task).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: At the circuit level, the dynamics of target selection are dictated by the relative strengths of the exogenous and endogenous activations and their congruency in space and time.
source: That is, these two independent response components explained the evolving attentional pointer observed during a typical antisaccade trial. This indicates that, at the circuit level, the dynamics of target selection are dictated by the relative strengths of the exogenous and endogenous activations and their congruency in space and time, however such activations are generated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study and the authors' interpretation.

claim: Temporal dependencies are much more accurately resolved when the fixation requirement is removed earlier and processing time is considered (instead of RT).
source: A critical conclusion from our work is that temporal dependencies are much more accurately resolved when the fixation requirement is removed earlier and processing time is considered (instead of RT).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental approach and results.

claim: Prior studies have shown that the effect of salience on saccadic choices is transient.
source: Prior studies have shown that the effect of salience on saccadic choices is transient (Donk and van Zoest, 2008; Siebold et al., 2011; Anderson et al., 2015), that stimulus-driven and goal-driven control signals on visual selection are distinct and can be temporally dissociated (van Zoest et al., 2004), and that in the transition between them there is a moment of ambiguity wherein choices are dictated by neither (van Heusden et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spatial attention dynamics in oculomotor circuits can vary more rapidly and abruptly than is generally appreciated.
source: The broader lesson is that spatial attention dynamics in oculomotor circuits can vary more rapidly and abruptly than is generally appreciated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental results.

claim: Saccades can go from being predominantly triggered in one direction to predominantly triggered in the opposite direction easily within 30–50 ms.
source: Saccades can go from being predominantly triggered in one direction to predominantly triggered in the opposite direction easily within 30–50 ms, and more than one such shift may occur in sequence (Figure 2c and d, Figure 2—figure supplement 2c and d, Figure 2—figure supplement 4c) as a consequence of distinct mechanisms interacting.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Eighteen human participants (11 female, 7 male) with a median age of 28 years (range, 24–63) were recruited and performed all four experiments.
source: Eighteen human participants (11 female, 7 male) were recruited and performed all four experiments (Methods). Thus, each participant generated data and a corresponding tachometric curve from two trial types (pro or anti) times four experiments for a total of eight experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental participants.

claim: The exogenous response window was set to 83–124 ms based on the tachometric curves from the reliable performers.
source: This exogenous response window was set to 83–124 ms based on the tachometric curves from the reliable performers (Figure 3a and c, shaded areas).
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the experimental data.

claim: The rise point from pro trials was 165 ms (in [158, 172] ms, 95% CI from bootstrap), whereas for anti trials it was 194 ms (in [191, 196] ms) when pooling data from Experiments 1 and 2.
source: Via sigmoidal fits, rise points were obtained for each of these curves (Figure 4d, vertical lines). Computed this way, the rise point from pro trials was 165 ms (in [158, 172] ms, 95% CI from bootstrap), whereas for anti trials it was 194 ms (in [191, 196] ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The rise point for pro trials was 152 ms (in [146, 157] ms, 95% CI), for anti trials it was 187 ms (in [185, 189] ms), and the difference was 35 ms when pooling data from Experiments 3 and 4.
source: In this case, the rise point for pro trials was 152 ms (in [146, 157] ms, 95% CI), for anti trials it was 187 ms (in [185, 189] ms), and the difference was 35 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The differences in processing time between pro and anti trials were 24 ms for the aggregate curves from Experiments 1 and 2, and 34 ms for the aggregate curves from Experiments 3 and 4 when using a fixed performance criterion of 70% correct.
source: These analyses were based on the rise points of the fitted sigmoidal functions, but results were very similar when using a fixed performance criterion of 70% correct to define the typical processing time required to make an informed choice (Methods). In that case, the differences in processing time between pro and anti trials were 24 ms for the aggregate curves from Experiments 1 and 2, and 34 ms for the aggregate curves from Experiments 3 and 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by alternative analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The informed antisaccades were consistently delayed even in Experiment 4, in which motor plans were strongly biased toward the non-cue by the early exogenous signal.
source: Most notably, the informed antisaccades were consistently delayed even in Experiment 4, in which motor plans were strongly biased toward the non-cue by the early exogenous signal (Figure 3c, Figure 2—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Producing an informed antisaccade required about 30 ms more of processing time than producing a similarly informed prosaccade, but this number varied by an additional amount in proportion to the strength of the initial bias toward or away from the cue.
source: So, in general, producing an informed antisaccade required about 30 ms more of processing time than producing a similarly informed prosaccade, but this number varied by an additional amount in proportion to the strength of the initial bias toward or away from the cue.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the relationship between processing-time cost and motor bias.

claim: In Experiment 4, pro trials demonstrate significantly higher accuracy than anti trials in the transition range in spite of the fact that, during the preceding capture interval, pro trials were at a huge disadvantage.
source: Again, the most notable result is for Experiment 4: in that case, pro trials demonstrate significantly higher accuracy than anti trials in the transition range (Figure 7e, orange points) in spite of the fact that, during the preceding capture interval, pro trials were at a huge disadvantage (Figure 7d; compare blue vs. red bars in C and T ranges).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d and 7e.

claim: The main consequence of the motor bias was to induce an asymmetry in timing and accuracy between pro- and antisaccades.
source: Thus, the bias did not incur an obvious disadvantage in terms of average success in the task. Its main consequence was simply to induce an asymmetry in timing and accuracy between pro- and antisaccades (Figures 6c and 7f).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of the relationship between motor bias and performance.
